examples.problem_statement: Recently, while shopping in Meena Market in Lucknow, I came across two new trousers selling at a discount. I decided to buy one of them for my little boy Sherry. The shopkeeper offered me the first trouser for ₹ 42 and said that it usually sold for 8/7 of that price. He then offered me the other trouser for ₹ 36 and said that it usually sold for 7/6th of that price. Of the two trousers which one do you think is a better bargain and what is the percentage discount on it? (a) first trouser, 12.5%  (b) second trouser, 14.28%  (c) Both are same  (d) None of these

solution.result: usual (marked) price of the first trouser is ₹ 48
solution.description: Apply the shopkeeper's ratio 8/7 to the first trouser's offer price of ₹ 42 to recover the price it usually sells for.
Subtract the offer price from the usual price to get the rupee discount, then express that discount as a fraction of the usual price ₹ 48.

solution.result: usual (marked) price of the second trouser is ₹ 42
solution.description: Do the same for the second trouser: apply its ratio 7/6 to the offer price of ₹ 36 to recover its usual selling price.
Take the rupee discount on the second trouser and express it as a fraction of its usual price ₹ 42, which is a smaller base than ₹ 48.

solution.result: the second trouser is the better bargain
solution.description: Compare the two discount percentages; the same ₹ 6 saved off the smaller base gives the larger percentage discount, so the second trouser wins.

key_reminders: "Usually sold for 8/7 of that price" means the offer price is multiplied by the fraction to get the marked price, not divided.
Percentage discount is always taken on the usual (marked) price, never on the discounted offer price.
Equal rupee savings do not mean equal discounts — the smaller base yields the bigger percentage.
common_mistakes: Seeing the identical ₹ 6 saving on both trousers and concluding the two bargains are the same (option c).
Dividing by 8/7 or 7/6 instead of multiplying, which turns ₹ 42 into ₹ 36.75 and destroys both discounts.
Computing 6/42 for the first trouser and 6/48 for the second by pairing each discount with the wrong base, which swaps the answer to (a).
